claims.text: Effective valence electron count primarily governs superconducting behavior in transition-metal high-entropy alloys rather than compositional disorder alone.
The proposed material class is body-centered cubic and consists of early- to mid-transition metals such as Nb, Ti, Zr, Ta, and Hf.
These high-entropy alloys have substantial atomic-scale compositional disorder.
Composition can be varied so as to change effective valence electron count while retaining approximately the same mixing entropy, disorder, and crystal structure.
Local atomic arrangement modulates the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Changing effective valence electron count alters the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the density of states at the Fermi level modify electron-phonon coupling strength within a BCS framework.
Stronger electron-phonon coupling increases the superconducting transition temperature.
Stronger electron-phonon coupling increases the upper critical field.
The relevant Ta-Nb-Zr-Hf-Ti high-entropy alloy family exhibits dirty-limit superconductivity.
Higher effective valence electron count will produce a higher superconducting transition temperature under otherwise similar disorder conditions.
Higher effective valence electron count will produce a greater upper critical field under otherwise similar disorder conditions.
Observed transition-temperature variations in the studied Ta-Nb-Zr-Hf-Ti films cannot be explained by disorder effects.
Binary Nb-Ti alloys provide a conventional-superconductor baseline with lower density-of-states modifications.
The proposed relationship is restricted to body-centered-cubic HEAs made from transition metals on the left side of the d-block.
The proposed relationship is restricted to a dirty-limit regime in which scattering is significant but does not solely determine superconducting behavior.
Subtle local structural inhomogeneities could influence superconducting properties.
Density of states at the Fermi level can be assessed by photoemission spectroscopy in the proposed comparison.
Electron-phonon coupling constants can be inferred from specific-heat-jump or tunneling measurements.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says valence electron count primarily governs superconductivity, whereas the falsification rule tests whether it solely governs superconductivity. This changes the causal standard and could reject a weaker primary-driver hypothesis merely because secondary influences exist.
